questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the literal meaning of dào wǒ zhèr lái?
What do the plurals wǒmen zhèr and nǐmen nàr often refer to?
What do the singular wǒ zhèr, nǐ nàr, and tā nàr usually refer to?
What does the verb dào require as its object?
What do zhèr and nàr do to wǒ and Wáng Xiānsheng?
Write the Chinese for "Go over there to Mr. Wáng."
Write the Chinese for "Where shall we meet?"
Which other verb also requires a place word as its object?
Write the Chinese for "Please come over here at two o'clock. All right?"

answers.answer_text: Liǎngdiǎn zhōng qǐng ni dào wǒ zhèr lái, xíng bu xíng?

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "See you tomorrow at two o'clock."

articles.text:
7. A: Zài nǎr jiàn ne?               Where shall we meet?
   B: Liǎngdiǎn zhōng qǐng ni dào    Please come over here at two o'clock.
      wǒ zhèr lái, xíng bu xíng?      All right?
   A: Hǎo. Míngtian liǎngdiǎn        Okay. See you tomorrow at two o'clock.
      zhōng jiàn.

Notes on No. 7

Dào wǒ zhèr lái means, literally, "come over to the place where I am." While plurals such as wǒmen zhèr and nǐmen nàr often refer to institutions, the singular wǒ zhèr, nǐ nàr, and tā nàr usually refer to any place where a person might be. In an office shared by two people, for instance, you could say Wǒ zhèr méiyou Yīng-Hàn zìdiǎn; nín nàr yǒu méiyou? "I don't have an English-Chinese dictionary over here; do you have one over there?"

Dào, like zài, is a verb which requires a place word as its object. Sentences like "Come over here to me" and "Go over there to Mr. Wáng" must be translated as Dào wǒ zhèr lái and Dào Wáng Xiānsheng nàr qù. Zhèr and nàr make wǒ and Wáng Xiānsheng parts of place-word phrases.
